turns.q:
Your response was: "Looked at it. Most of it made sense. One thing didn't — two buttons at the bottom. Went to the wrong one first. Darker one drew my eye. That wasn't the action I needed."

We want to understand what you meant by "went to the wrong one first", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The two bottom buttons are stacked with “Continue Shopping” placed above “Place Order,” making the upper button look like the primary next step in the checkout layout.  
B) The “Continue Shopping” button is visually more prominent than “Place Order,” so the hierarchy suggests it is the main action on the screen.  
C) The bottom area does not clearly separate the secondary navigation option from the checkout completion action, so the two actions feel grouped as equivalent choices.  
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
What specifically about the bottom button area makes “Continue Shopping” read as the stronger action than “Place Order” in this layout?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping.' Heavier. More presence. 'Place Order' is the lighter one.

turns.q: Would that hierarchy make the checkout completion action harder to locate, or would it mainly make the intended next step ambiguous once someone sees both bottom buttons?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' pulled the eye every scan. 'Place Order' didn't. Almost went the wrong direction. Re-read both before I moved.

turns.q: If this exact bottom area were shown to someone ready to finish checkout, would the darker “Continue Shopping” button create a momentary pause, or could it send them toward the wrong next step entirely?
turns.a: Said it. Both competing. Looked at the wrong one.

turns.q: What would the correct version of that bottom area look like so the eye goes to “Place Order” first instead of “Continue Shopping”?
turns.a: 'Place Order': solid fill, brand color, white label text — standard primary button. 'Continue Shopping': no fill, border only or underlined text — standard secondary treatment. Contrast between the two carries the hierarchy signal. Right now they're competing at similar fill weight with the wrong one winning. One pass, two buttons, done.
